title: Build vs buy AI: which should your firm do for each workflow?
description: For each workflow at a 40-500 person firm: when to buy AI, configure a platform, build your own or wait, with dated prices and sign-offs.
topic: Build vs buy AI: which should your firm do?
job: decide whether to build an AI tool, buy one, or buy and adapt
verdict: Buy if the job is common, like drafting or meeting notes: check the AI in tools you already pay for[^21][^24].
Buy a platform and configure it if the job is common but the steps are yours, like staff policy questions[^1][^23].
Build if your own data or process is the edge, no product fits, and someone owns the upkeep[^6][^25].
Do neither yet if you can't name one measure, one owner and data that's ready[^7][^8].
Whichever you pick, a named person signs off anything the tool tells customers or posts to the books[^31][^35].

summary: Buying gets a product, configuring adapts a platform to your steps, while building on a rented model gives control but leaves upkeep to you[^6][^23][^25]. Most firms now buy: 76% of enterprise AI use cases in 2025, per investor Menlo Ventures[^3][^4]. People and process decide the result more than the model[^13][^12].

recipes.name: 1. Buy for a common job: drafting and summaries for 100 staff
recipes.when: Pick it when the job is the same at every firm and a plan you can buy already does it[^21][^24]. Most firms start here[^3].
flow: Ops lead: pick one workflow and one measure, such as time to first draft[^8][^12]
IT lead: turn on the business AI plan your firm already fits[^19][^21][^24]
Security lead: check the no-training and data-retention terms in writing[^19][^20][^24]
Team leads: run a 30-day trial and record the measure
Business owner: keep it, change it or drop it
recipes.cost: 100 seats: $24,000 a year on ChatGPT Business billed yearly, or $25,200 for the Microsoft 365 Copilot Business add-on at list[^19][^21]. Prices read 26 Nov 2026; Google Workspace plans already include Gemini[^24].

recipes.name: 2. Configure a platform: an agent for staff policy questions
recipes.when: Pick it when the job is common but the steps, documents or rules are yours. MIT found successful buyers demanded tools fitted to their process[^1].
flow: Process owner: write down the steps and where the answers live[^7][^12]
Data owner: fix access rights so each person sees only what they may see[^30]
IT lead: build the agent in a platform you already license, such as Copilot Studio, and launch it to one team first[^23]
Named reviewer: check a sample of answers weekly and own the corrections[^31][^34]
Ops lead: track the measure for 90 days, the pace MIT saw from mid-market leaders[^1]
recipes.cost: Copilot Studio is $200 a month per 25,000 credits, or pay-as-you-go, read 26 Nov 2026[^23]. Credits used vary per action, so pilot on real traffic before you commit[^23].

recipes.name: 3. Build a narrow tool: supplier documents into your ERP (enterprise resource planning) system
recipes.when: Pick it when your own data or process is the edge and no product does the job[^6][^1]. Get the data ready first: Gartner expects 60% of projects without AI-ready data to be dropped[^7].
flow: Business owner: confirm no product fits and your data is the edge[^1][^6]
Build team, in-house or outside: call a rented model from your own tool[^16][^17]
Build team: add tests, monitoring and a tested fallback model[^25][^26]
AP (accounts payable) lead: approve anything the tool posts to the ERP above a set value[^35]
IT lead: track the model's retirement date and re-test before the cut-off[^27][^28]
recipes.cost: Model use for 2,000 documents a month: about $60 on a $2/$10 model, or $3 on a $0.10/$0.50 model (our arithmetic)[^16][^17]. Integration, testing and upkeep cost far more than tokens[^25][^26].

humanRole: Ops lead or process owner: defines the human checks and signs them off before launch. NIST's AI framework asks that human oversight be defined, assessed and documented[^34].
A named approver signs off any high-impact action the tool proposes, such as an ERP posting or a refund. OWASP lists unchecked AI actions as a top risk[^35].
AI drafts, people decide: support agents with AI resolved 15% more issues an hour, and newer agents gained most[^36]. In a P&G study, human judgment kept its value in picking the best option[^37].
A named person owns what any chatbot tells customers. A tribunal held Air Canada liable for its chatbot's wrong answer[^31][^32].

ownData.title: How much notice do vendors give before a model or tool goes away?
ownData.intro: On 26 Nov 2026 we read OpenAI's and Anthropic's deprecation pages and logged each notice rule and dated retirement[^27][^28]. We counted the days from notice to shut-off ourselves. Anything you build or configure must be moved and re-tested inside that window.
rows: A build on a stable model gets about half a year to move
Niche models give you half the time
Don't run real work on a preview model
Tools built on these must move to a newer model by then
A platform you configure can be retired too, not just a model
About two months to move and re-test
Not found on the page we read[^28]
Ask for a notice period in writing before you build
ownData.note: Zavient check of two vendors' public pages, read 26 Nov 2026; Microsoft and Google were not part of this check. Days are our arithmetic from the dated notices. Policies change, so re-check before you build.

example.input: Illustrative: a 150-person firm weighs three workflows. Staff want help drafting client emails. HR wants an agent for policy questions, and AP wants supplier documents read into the ERP.
example.output: Emails: buy, using the AI in the suite the firm already pays for[^21][^24]. Policy questions: configure an agent on a licensed platform, after fixing access rights[^23][^30]. Supplier documents: build only if no product fits, at about $60 a month in model use plus upkeep[^16][^25].

watchOuts: Starting a pilot with no business measure: Gartner names unclear value as a top reason GenAI projects are dropped[^5][^8]. Set one measure and one owner before day one.

Building for a common job: drafting and search are already inside suites firms pay for[^21][^24]. Check what you license first; in MIT's interviews, bought tools reached deployment about twice as often[^1][^2].
Data that isn't ready: Gartner expects 60% of projects without AI-ready data to be dropped through 2026[^7]. Test on your real documents before you sign or build[^10].
Forgetting the model will be retired: OpenAI gives as little as 2 weeks' notice on previews and 6 months on stable models[^27]. Track the dates and keep a tested fallback model[^28].
No access controls: 97% of firms with an AI breach lacked them, in an IBM-sponsored study[^30]. Give staff an approved tool, since workers at 90%+ of firms use personal AI anyway[^1].

Lenders citing old model rules: SR 26-2 replaced SR 11-7 on 17 Apr 2026, and it is aimed at banks over $30B in assets[^33]. Smaller lenders should still keep a list of every model, bought or built, and check each one.

faq.q: Do most companies buy AI tools or build their own?
faq.a: Most buy: Menlo Ventures, an AI investor, found 76% of enterprise AI use cases were bought in 2025, up from 53% in 2024[^3][^4]. Wharton found about a third of GenAI tech budgets still go to internal research and development[^14].

faq.q: Should we build or buy AI agents?
faq.a: Buy or configure first, unless your data or process is the edge[^1][^6]. MIT found bought or partnered tools reached deployment about twice as often as internal builds. The split comes from interviews, as the report itself says[^1][^2].

faq.q: Should I learn to build it, pay someone, or buy?
faq.a: For most owner-run firms, buy first and spend your time on the workflow. If you pay someone to build, budget for upkeep: Google engineers found maintaining machine learning (ML) systems is the hard, costly part[^25][^26].

faq.q: Is enterprise knowledge search worth building?
faq.a: No, not from scratch: search across your files now comes in Microsoft 365 Copilot and Google Workspace plans[^21][^24]. The hard part either way is access rights, so each person sees only what they may see[^30].

faq.q: How long until we see value?
faq.a: Weeks for a bought tool, months for a build. Gartner's survey averaged 8 months from prototype to production[^9]. MIT saw mid-market leaders go from pilot to full rollout in about 90 days[^1].

faq.q: Should companies build AI, buy AI or assemble AI?
faq.a: Buy or assemble most AI, and build only where your own data or process is the edge.[^1][^6] Assembling means configuring a platform you license, like Copilot Studio, for steps that are yours.[^23] Gartner found embedding AI in apps you already use was the most common approach.[^9]

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy when the job is common, you have no build team, and the vendor's data terms meet your rules[^6][^20]. Most firms do: 76% of enterprise AI use cases were bought in 2025, per Menlo Ventures, an AI investor[^3]. MIT found bought tools reached deployment about twice as often, from interviews rather than market data[^1][^2].
buyVsBuild.build: Build when your own data or process is the edge and you need control of the rules[^6][^1]. Gartner's 2024 enterprise guide puts training a model from scratch at $8M-20M upfront[^6]. A firm your size builds a narrow tool on a rented model instead, and budgets for upkeep and model retirements[^16][^27].

pickElse: The AI in your current suite already does the job: Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace plans include it[^21][^24]. Turn it on for one team before you buy anything new.
The process itself is broken: fix the steps or the data first. RAND found misunderstood problems and missing data among the root causes of failed AI projects[^10].
The job is a score or forecast from your own records: use a predictive model, not a chatbot. Gartner advises defining where generative AI should not be used[^8].
No one can check the output and an error would be costly: keep the decision with people for now. Most failed projects lacked risk controls or clear value, per Gartner[^5].

offer.heading: Not sure whether to build or buy for your top workflow?
offer.body: Buy for most workflows; configure a platform when the steps are yours, and build only when your own data or process is the edge. In a free 30-minute call, we tell you which applies to the one workflow you most want fixed, plus the measure to track.

keyword.note: 'build vs buy ai' itself is 30 searches a month at $18 a click, just under the $20 niche gate, so the broader phrase carries the demand.

reviews.notes: Wants to know, per workflow, whether to buy, configure or build, how long each takes and who does what. The three recipes name a role on every step, and the bottom line gives four 'if' rules plus a sign-off rule. Fix: the buy column's 'days to weeks' was footnoted to a Google Cloud survey that measures idea-to-production, not seat roll-outs; it now says plainly it is our estimate. FAQ questions were seen at: r/AI_Agents (build or buy agents; learn, pay someone or buy), r/ArtificialInteligence (build, buy or assemble), r/vectordatabase (knowledge search), Quora (do most companies buy). Forum threads are not used as evidence.

Reads on a phone. 'Tokens' is now glossed as word pieces in the side-by-side table. 'Deprecated' was unclear and, for Agent Builder, read as past tense four days early; the table now says OpenAI has set it for retirement on 30 Nov 2026, and the own-data row says 'set for retirement'. Shadow AI is explained in the same cell as personal AI tools staff use anyway.

Asks whether one team can try it first and what it costs the unit. Recipe 1 already had a 30-day trial; recipe 2 now launches the agent to one team first. Cash costs are dated vendor prices with our arithmetic labelled. The research has no sourced figure for staff time on a build, so none is given; the cost lines say integration and upkeep outweigh tokens.

Read as the AP lead or controller for recipe 3, and as a head of lending. AP lead approves ERP postings above a set value. A lender would ask what the examiner expects: the EU AI Act watch-out was swapped for SR 26-2, which replaced SR 11-7 on 17 Apr 2026 and targets banks over $30B, so smaller lenders don't over-read it. The EU rule stays in Useful resources.

Steve gets the answer from the title and five 'if' bullets. The Gartner cost table looked like a quote for his firm; it is retitled 'Why don't firms your size train their own model?' and says it is 2024 enterprise data. The 'pay someone' FAQ now uses the forum's real wording and answers it without naming any firm. The MIT split is labelled interview-based everywhere it appears, and the page says no study covers 40-500 person firms. Example marked illustrative.

answers.recipes: Buy for a common job, configure a platform when the steps are yours, and build only when your own data or process is the edge.[^21][^1][^6]
answers.human-role: A named person signs off anything the tool tells customers or posts to the books, and the ops lead defines those checks before launch.[^31][^35][^34] AI drafts; people decide.[^36]
answers.example: At an illustrative 150-person firm, client emails get a bought tool, policy questions get a configured agent, and supplier documents get a narrow build only if no product fits.[^21][^23][^16]
answers.what-goes-wrong: Teams most often start with no business measure, build what their suite already does, or skip getting their data ready.[^5][^21][^7]
answers.something-else: Pick neither when your suite already does it, the process is broken, the job is a score or forecast from your records, or no one can check the output.[^21][^10][^8][^5]
answers.table-1: Buying is quickest, at $20-31.50 a user a month. Configuring a platform takes weeks to a few months; building your own averages 8 months to production.[^19][^18][^22][^1][^9] Building also costs far more in upkeep than in model fees.[^25][^26]
answers.table-2: Training a model from scratch costs $8M-20M upfront in Gartner's enterprise figures, against $100K-200K to buy a ready tool.[^6] For a 40-500 person firm, that puts training your own model out of reach.
answers.table-3: Bought or partnered tools reached deployment about 67% of the time in MIT's 2025 study, against about 33% for internal builds.[^1][^2] Most firms now buy: 76% of enterprise AI use cases in Menlo's 2025 survey.[^3]
answers.own-data: OpenAI promises at least 6 months' notice for stable models, 3 months for specialized ones and as little as 2 weeks for previews.[^27] Anthropic retired Claude Sonnet 4.5 on 61 days' notice.[^28]
